purpose: Amiloride helps your body get rid of extra fluid and salt through your urine, which can reduce swelling and lower blood pressure. It is often used along with other water pills to help prevent your potassium levels from dropping too low. Your doctor may prescribe it for heart failure, high blood pressure, or liver disease.
how_it_works: Your kidneys control how much salt and water stay in your body. Amiloride works by blocking a channel in your kidneys that normally reabsorbs sodium, so more sodium and water leave your body in your urine. Unlike most other water pills, it helps your body hold onto potassium at the same time, which is important for your heart and muscles.
common_side_effects: You might notice increased urination, especially when you first start the medication. Some people experience nausea, stomach upset, headache, or dizziness. Less commonly, you may feel tired or have muscle cramps.
warnings: The biggest concern with amiloride is that it can cause your potassium levels to get too high, which can be dangerous for your heart. Avoid taking potassium supplements or eating very large amounts of high-potassium foods like bananas or oranges without asking your doctor first. Tell your doctor if you have kidney problems, as this medication may not be safe for you. Also let your doctor know all other medications you take, since some drugs like ACE inhibitors or certain blood pressure medicines can also raise potassium levels.
typical_dosing: The usual starting dose for adults is 5 mg once a day, taken with food to reduce stomach upset. Your doctor may increase this to 10 mg per day if needed. Always take it exactly as your doctor prescribes and do not stop without talking to them first.
